items.title: Rational-local quantum halves and torus specialize at q=1
items.statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]), and
$R:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q-1)}\subset\mathbb Q(q)$, so that $R$ is a DVR with
uniformizer $q-1$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]). Let
$U_R:=U_A\otimes_AR$ be the base
change of the integral form $U_A$ of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], identified with its image in
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$.

(a) **Halves.** Each root component $U_R^\pm[\pm\nu]$ is a finite free
$R$-module, generated as an $R$-module by ordinary words
$E_{i_1}\cdots E_{i_k}$ (respectively $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$) of degree
$\pm\nu$, and its $q=1$ fibre $U_R^\pm[\pm\nu]\otimes_RR/(q-1)$ is the classical
half $U(\mathfrak n^\pm)_{\mathbb Q}[\pm\nu]$ of the Kac-Moody algebra,
presented by the separate classical Serre relations
([[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]](i),
[[thm-serre-presentation-of-a-kac-moody-algebra]]).

(b) **Torus.** Write $H_i:=T_{i,0,1}$ and let $L=\sum_i\mathbb Z(d_ih_i)$.
Then $U_R^0$ has the $R$-basis
$\{K_c\prod_iK_i^{\delta_i}H_i^{t_i}\}$ with $\delta_i\in\{0,1\}$,
$t_i\ge0$ and $c$ running through the explicit representatives of
$P^{\vee}/L$ of
[[lem-unmodified-integral-torus-has-a-quantum-binomial-basis]](b); and
multiplication
$U_R^-\otimes_RU_R^0\otimes_RU_R^+\to U_R$ is an isomorphism of
$R$-modules.

(c) **Positive quotient.** For every characteristic-zero field $k$ (an
$A$-algebra via $q\mapsto1$), the positive toral quotient
$U_A^0\otimes_Ak/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is the polynomial algebra $k[H_i:i\in I]$
with, in it, $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c}{t}$; and the positive full quotient
$(U_A\otimes_Ak)/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is isomorphic to $U(\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}})_k$,
where $\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}}$ is the classical Lie algebra presented by the
generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ with the Cartan and Serre relations, its Cartan being
the span of the independent simple coroots. This is an assertion about the
stated quotient only: it is not claimed that $K_h=1$ in the unquotiented
specialization $U_A\otimes_Ak$, where genuine toral characters such as
$K=-1$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ survive. Direct substitution $q=1$ into the
vanishing denominators $q_i^s-q_i^{-s}$ is never performed.
items.strategy: A nonzero rational function has a unique integer order at q=1 and a unit factor; every ideal of R has a least such order and is generated by that power of q-1, proving the DVR/PID property. R localizes A by inverting nonzero integers and polynomials nonzero at1, so flat localization identifies U_A⊗R with its image. Every [r]_i! has nonzero value r! and is an R-unit; hence U_R^± is generated by ordinary E_i/F_i. Fixed root degree has finitely many words, so its component is finite generated and torsionfree inside the field half and thus R-free. Its rank is the generic half dimension, equal to the classical dimension by the published rank supplier (the declared AC use). Quantum Serre relations specialize and give a surjection from the classical half; equal finite dimensions make it an isomorphism degreewise. For the torus, the integral identity [t]_iT_{i,c,t}=(q_i^{c-t+1}H_i+K_i^-1[c-t+1]_i)T_{i,c,t-1} implies U_R^0 is generated by K_h and H_i, since [t]_i is an R-unit. In the independent simple torus L=Σ_i Z(d_i h_i), its presentation is R[H_i,K_i]/(K_i^2-(q_i-q_i^-1)K_iH_i-1). Each monic quadratic gives a free polynomial-H module with basis K_i^delta_i. It injects in Q(q)[L]: over the fraction field solve H_i=(K_i-K_i^-1)/(q_i-q_i^-1), and the monic presentation is torsionfree over R. Choose a finite coordinate summand of Pvee containing all d_i h_i; in each of its cosets of L choose minimal coordinate absolute-value sum, breaking finite ties lexicographically, and retain the complementary coordinates. This gives explicit coset representatives without an arbitrary family choice. The group algebra decomposes over these cosets, giving the displayed R-basis of the full toral algebra. Triangular spanning is the reordering lemma. All factor modules are now R-free (the halves are direct sums of their finite free components), so their tensor product is torsionfree; field triangular decomposition proves injectivity. At q=1 and K_h=1, the same toral recursion gives t Tbar_{i,c,t}=(H_i+c-t+1)Tbar_{i,c,t-1}, so Tbar=binom(H_i+c,t). The local toral basis/presentation gives no other relation among H_i. Alternatively evaluate the torus on all integral characters phi:Pvee→Z: H_i evaluates to phi(h_i); independence of h_i makes these values contain a full-rank integer subgroup of Z^I, which is Zariski dense in characteristic zero. Thus polynomial independence and the exact toral kernel are proved. The mixed relation gives [E_i,F_j]=δ_ijH_i, and T_{i,0,1}E_j=E_jT_{i,a_ij,1} specializes to [H_i,E_j]=a_ijE_j (similarly F_j). Serre and toral relations therefore give a surjection from the classical derived enveloping algebra. Both algebras have the same negative-toral-positive vector decomposition (classical PBW/Serre and the proved local triangular decomposition), so that map is an isomorphism. The extra classical Cartan directions are reconstructed on graded modules, not falsely added as algebra generators to this positive quotient.

items.title: The negative-half bilinear form is symmetric, nondegenerate and integral
items.statement:
Let $U_q^-=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}U_q^-[-\nu]$ be the negative half of the
Drinfeld-Jimbo algebra of a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), with skew derivations
$e_i',e_i''$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]),
and let $(\ ,\ )$ be a bilinear form on $U_q^-$.

(i) **Existence and symmetry.** A bilinear form with $(1,1)=1$ and
$(F_iP,Q)=(P,e_i'(Q))$ for all $i,P,Q$ exists on $U_q^-$; every normalized
homogeneous form satisfying these conditions is symmetric; and by the
uniqueness of [[def-the-lusztig-kashiwara-bilinear-form-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]
there is exactly one such form. No separate right-adjunction formula for
$(P,QF_i)$ is asserted: in the rank-one subalgebra a formula
$(P,QF_i)=c\,(e_i''P,Q)$ with constant $c$ is false, as the explicit values in
(iv) show.

(ii) **Orthogonality.** $(U_q^-[-\nu],U_q^-[-\mu])=0$ whenever $\nu\ne\mu$.

(iii) **Nondegeneracy.** For every $0\ne x\in U_q^-$ there is $y\in U_q^-$ with
$(x,y)\ne0$; equivalently, the restriction of the form to each
finite-dimensional graded piece $U_q^-[-\nu]$ is nondegenerate.

(iv) **Integrality on the word lattice.** Let $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) and let $W\subseteq U_A^-$ be the
$A$-span of the monomials $F_{i_1}\cdots F_{i_k}$ ($k\ge0$). Then
$W\subseteq U_A^-$ (because $F_i^k=[k]_i!F_i^{(k)}$ and $[k]_i!\in A$), and
$(W,W)\subseteq A$. On the larger divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ the form is
*not* $A$-valued: in the rank-one subalgebra generated by a single $F_i$ one
has, for all $a,b\ge0$,
$$(F_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)})=\delta_{ab}\frac{q_i^{-a(a-1)/2}}{[a]_i!}=\delta_{ab}\frac{1}{[a]_{q_i^2}!},$$
in particular $(F_i^{(2)},F_i^{(2)})=1/(1+q_i^2)\notin A$; here
$[a]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{m=1}^a(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(m-1)})$. Globally, with
$A_{\mathrm{loc}}=A[s^{-1}:s\in S]$, the localization of $A$ inverting the
multiplicative set $S$ generated by $\{[r]_i!:i\in I,r\ge1\}$ (equivalently inverting the
Gaussian factorials $[r]_{q_i^2}!$), one has
$(U_A^-,U_A^-)\subseteq A_{\mathrm{loc}}$: divided-power words are word
vectors divided by finite products of these factorials. This is an exact
denominator bound, not an $A$-integrality assertion on $U_A^-$ in this
normalization.
items.strategy: The separation lemma constructs the form explicitly from the proved generic Hopf pairing by color-degree scaling c_nu=∏(q_i-q_i^-1)^{nu_i}. Its matching-permutation Gram formula proves symmetry and e'-adjunction, and the generic pairing proves descent and nondegeneracy on each actual Serre-quotient component. The form Definition now imposes homogeneity, so uniqueness follows by first-letter peeling. This transport is degree dependent, not one scalar multiplying the whole form. Orthogonality is its homogeneous construction. Alternatively, repeated skew separation and adjunction pair a nonzero x with an appropriate first-letter word; reverse the chosen derivation order correctly when writing that word. For integrality on W, each skew deletion coefficient is a Laurent q-power in A. Height induction therefore gives B(W,W)⊂A. A divided-power word is its underlying ordinary word divided by ∏[r]_i!, giving B(U_A^-,U_A^-)⊂A_loc by bilinearity. In rank one e_i'F_i^(n)=q_i^{-(n-1)}F_i^(n-1). Since F_i^(n)=[n]_i^-1 F_iF_i^(n-1), its squared norm obeys b_n=q_i^{-(n-1)}b_{n-1}/[n]_i, starting b_0=1. Thus b_n=q_i^{-n(n-1)/2}/[n]_i!=1/[n]_{q_i^2}! and different powers are orthogonal. At n=2 this is 1/(1+q_i^2), not in A, proving the exact native correction. No integrality on the whole divided-power lattice is claimed without the stated localization. AC is inherited only from the generic pairing/separation supplier.

items.title: The q=1 toral specialization identifies the classical Cartan generators
items.statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum, let
$U_A$ be the integral form with toral part $U_A^0$
([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]) and let $k$ be a
characteristic-zero field regarded as an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$.
Write $H_i:=T_{i,0,1}$ and $\bar x$ for the image of $x$ in a specialization.

(a) **Algebra level.** The positive toral quotient
$U_A^0\otimes_Ak/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is the polynomial algebra
$k[H_i:i\in I]$, and in it $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c}{t}$ for all
$c\in\mathbb Z$, $t\ge0$
([[lem-rational-local-quantum-halves-and-torus-specialize-at-q-one]](c)).
No residual $K_h$-ambiguity remains after this quotient — the ideal
$(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is exactly the kernel of the comparison with
$k[H_i]$ — but it is *not* claimed that $K_h=1$ in the unquotiented
specialization $U_A^0\otimes_Ak$.

(b) **Label-graded lattices.** Let $M$ be a $P$-graded type-one
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module with label grading $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let
$M_A=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}(M_A\cap M_\mu)$ be a $U_A$-stable $A$-submodule that
is graded in the *lattice's own* sense, i.e. it is the direct sum of its
intersections with the label spaces. Then, on $M_A\otimes_Ak$, the operators
induced by $E_i,F_i$ (and all of $U_A$) satisfy: $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$ for
every $h\in P^{\vee}$; $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ acts on the image of $M_A\cap M_\mu$ by
the integer $\binom{\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+c}{t}$; and
$[\bar E_i,\bar F_j]=\delta_{ij}\bar H_i$,
$[\bar H_i,\bar E_j]=a_{ij}\bar E_j$,
$[\bar H_i,\bar F_j]=-a_{ij}\bar F_j$, where $\bar H_i$ acts on the image of
$M_A\cap M_\mu$ by the integer $\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$.

The grading hypothesis in (b) is a real hypothesis on the lattice: it is not
inferred from the mere fact that $M_A$ spans a weight module. All divisions
that occur are performed inside the DVR
$R=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q-1)}$ (units $[r]_i!$ and $q_i^{\pm1}$); no vanishing
denominator $q_i^s-q_i^{-s}$ is substituted by $q=1$.
items.strategy: The rational-local half/torus theorem proves the algebra-level positive quotient and exact toral kernel using the integral recursion, monic local toral basis and polynomial independence. For lattice operators, diagonal K_h acts by q^{<mu,h>}; the lattice's actual grading ensures this equality applies to a spanning set of lattice vectors and hence specializes to1. The scalar T value is the integer Gaussian [<mu,h_i>+c choose t]_i with q_i=q^{d_i}, not a formula silently dropping d_i. Gaussian integrality gives its q=1 value as the ordinary integer binomial (including negative upper values). The mixed relation gives [E_i,F_j]=δ_ijH_i. The shifted toral identity H_iE_j=E_jT_{i,a_ij,1} and its F version give the remaining classical commutators after the positive quotient, or directly on each lattice weight. No naive division by q_i-q_i^-1 is specialized.

items.title: The integrable quantum highest weight module exists and is unique
items.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support contained in
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.
items.strategy: Apply the Serre-quotient integrability lemma to construct tilde L, prove nonzero top and local nilpotence, and obtain the universal map to any integrable cyclic highest module. The local q1 deformation lemma compares the finite DVR-free weight lattices in tilde L and its graded simple quotient L with the same classical simple module, giving equal dimensions and hence tilde L=L. The Cartan-projection lemma gives the normalized nondegenerate homogeneous form on L; its maximum-height raising argument proves ordinary simplicity even when an ordinary submodule is not assumed graded. Thus every nonzero quotient in the universal property is the same L. This closes the native gap and does not use a later global Z-basis as an early premise.

items.title: Integrable bounded-above quantum modules with finite-dimensional weight spaces are direct sums of simple highest weight modules
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module over $\mathbb Q(q)$ for a finite symmetrizable
Cartan datum such that

(a) $M$ is a weight module with $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu<\infty$ for every
$\mu\in P$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]);

(b) the weight set $\mathrm{wt}(M)$ is bounded above: it is contained in a
finite union $\bigcup_{j=1}^s(\lambda_j-Q_+)$;

(c) $M$ is integrable, i.e. $E_i$ and $F_i$ act locally nilpotently for every
$i$.

Then $M$ is isomorphic to an algebraic direct sum of simple integrable highest
weight modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in P^+$
([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]);
concretely, every nonzero submodule of $M$ contains a maximal vector $v$ whose
cyclic submodule $U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$ for some
$\lambda\in P^+$, and $M$ is the direct sum of the submodules generated by the
vectors of any maximal independent family of simple submodules. AC is used
exactly to select a maximal independent family of simple submodules
simultaneously; restricted to any module generated by one finite-dimensional
$U^{\ge0}$-submodule the decomposition is obtained by a finite induction and is
choice-free. The finite-cone modules use the explicit label grading, and the
regularization supplier is used when the original pairing is not separating
([[lem-finite-support-regularization-of-quantum-label-weight-modules]]).
items.strategy: Choose one finite-support regularization for the upper cones; it preserves the grading, all E/F actions and reconstructs the old torus, so prove the statement in the regular support category and transport back. For any vector, U^{≥0}v has finitely many weights: the upper set of each of its finitely many support labels inside the finite union of cones is finite, and each weight has finite dimension. An integrable cyclic highest submodule is the simple L(lambda) by the completed early universality theorem. For restricted duality use the Q(q)-linear anti-involution phi fixing the torus and interchanging E_i,F_i (tau composed with bar), on M^*=⊕_mu Hom(M_mu,Q(q)). Finite-dimensional weights give M=M^{**}. To verify integrability of the dual, each rank-one cyclic submodule in M is finite dimensional: commute its E/F powers into F^bE^a form, and use local nilpotence on the finitely many E^a v. The generic rank-one finite modules split into finite simple strings by their distinct Casimir scalars, with equal highest labels split by the top-vector bases. The finite sum U_iM_mu therefore captures every string contributing to the mu-coordinate and gives a uniform exponent for the transpose arrows into that coordinate; the dual is integrable. Fix a globally maximal weight lambda in a nonzero submodule, a vector v_lambda, and extend its evaluation functional to the full finite-dimensional M_lambda with value1 on v_lambda. This gives phi_lambda∈M^*_lambda (not merely a functional on V). Since no higher label exists, it is highest. Its cyclic W is L(lambda). Dualizing W→M^* gives M→W^*; its restriction to V=U_qv_lambda is nonzero on the top and hence an isomorphism between the simple highest modules. Invert that restriction to obtain a retraction M→V and split. If M=U_qF for finite-dimensional U^{≥0}-stable F, choose a maximal weight of F: it is globally maximal in M because multiplying negative words only lowers the finite weights of F. The retraction reduces the dimension of the generating image of F, giving finite induction. For arbitrary M every cyclic submodule is of that form, so M is a sum of simple submodules. Under AC select a maximal independent family of them (Zorn, or simultaneous singular bases) and prove it spans: a simple submodule not contained in the sum intersects it either in itself or zero, and the latter would enlarge the family. This yields the algebraic direct sum. The normalized sigma-form gives the equivalent self-dual identification; no nonexistent extension from V^* to M^* is asserted without explicitly choosing the functional in M_lambda. The commissioned finite rank-one Casimir/string argument is supplied locally from the published rank-one formulas. Upper-cone root coefficients bound each fixed simple-root line; finite strings bound its bottom, proving restricted-dual integrability without a global coroot bound. A maximal generating label need not dominate all other labels. Use the finite graded hull and finite-simple-sum argument for ordinary ungraded submodules; no prerequisite on the later QG3 page is introduced.

items.title: Specialization at q=1 recovers the classical enveloping relations
items.statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum, $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$,
$U_A$ the integral form of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], and $k$
a characteristic-zero field regarded as an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$. Let
$\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}}$ be the classical Lie algebra presented by
generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ with the Cartan and Serre relations, its Cartan being
the span of the independent simple coroots
([[thm-serre-presentation-of-a-kac-moody-algebra]]).

(a) **Halves.** $U_A^\pm\otimes_Ak\cong U(\mathfrak n^\pm)_k$ by
$F_i\mapsto f_i$, respectively $E_i\mapsto e_i$.

(b) **Positive quotient.** The quotient
$(U_A\otimes_Ak)/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is isomorphic to
$U(\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}})_k$; in it $\bar H_i=\bar T_{i,0,1}$ is the
classical coroot generator, $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c}{t}$, and the positive
toral quotient is $k[H_i:i\in I]$ with kernel exactly
$(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$.

(c) **Operator form.** On every $U_A$-stable label-graded lattice the quotient
action of (b) is automatic: $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$, the $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ act by
the integer binomials $\binom{\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+c}{t}$, and all classical
Cartan and Serre operator relations hold, without any unproved global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness.

(d) **Boundaries.** The unquotiented specialization $U_A\otimes_Ak$ is *not*
identified with $U(\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}})_k$: it retains toral characters,
as the integral $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-representation with $E=F=0$, $K=-1$ shows.
Extra Cartan directions of a regular realization act diagonally on
label-graded modules; they are not fabricated as generators of the toral
integral form, and direct substitution $q=1$ into vanishing denominators
$q_i^s-q_i^{-s}$ is never performed anywhere in this comparison.
items.strategy: Localize A to R=Q[q]_(q-1). This is flat and identifies the base-changed integral subalgebras with their actual generated images. Since every [r]_i! is an R-unit, each half is generated by ordinary generators; its finite DVR-free components and generic/classical rank comparison give the half isomorphisms after specialization. The local theorem proves the positive toral polynomial quotient, exact binomial identity and mixed/Cartan relations, then compares its negative-toral-positive vector decomposition with classical PBW to prove the full derived enveloping isomorphism. Tensoring with k changes only rational coefficients. The quotient by all K_h-1 is explicit; to see why it is essential, specialize the sl2 integral representation E=F=0,K=-1, whose toral binomial values are (-1)^t[c choose t]_q and retain K=-1 at1. On an actually graded stable lattice K_h acts by a Laurent scalar specializing to1, so the module factors through the positive quotient. All stronger algebra-level toral formulas missing from the native scaffold are now supplied, without unproved global Z-freeness.

items.title: The normalized type-A Hecke algebra and its bar involution
items.statement: Let n≥1 and A=Z[v±1]. For n≥2, H_v(n) is the type-A algebra with quadratic relation H_s²=1+(v⁻¹−v)H_s and the braid and distant-commutation relations; H_v(1)=A. With q=v⁻² and H_w=v^{ℓ(w)}T_w, the generic standard basis specializes and rescales to an A-basis, with H_wH_s=H_{ws} on length ascent and H_{ws}+(v⁻¹−v)H_w on descent. The bar assignment is semilinear, v↦v⁻¹ and H_s↦H_s⁻¹=H_s−(v⁻¹−v); its well-defined involution and value ι(H_w)=H_{w⁻¹}⁻¹ are supplied by lem-the-hecke-bar-involution-is-well-defined.
items.strategy: A definition item. (i) The coefficient base change q↦v⁻² and rescaling H_{s_i}=vT_i identify the two presentations; the reverse assignment is T_i=v⁻¹H_{s_i}. The standard-basis theorem gives the basis, and rescaling gives the displayed multiplication rule. (ii) The quadratic relation gives H_{s_i}^{-1}=H_{s_i}−(v⁻¹−v). (iii) The semilinear bar assignment is declared here; its descent and involutivity are proved by the assigned lemma. No Choice is used.

items.title: The Hecke bar involution is well defined
items.statement: In H_v(n) there is a unique A-semilinear unital ring involution ι with ι(v)=v⁻¹ and ι(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}⁻¹. It is multiplicative and satisfies ι²=id and ι(H_w)=H_{w⁻¹}⁻¹ for every w∈S_n; consequently each H_w is invertible and ι(H_{w⁻¹})=H_w⁻¹.
items.strategy: Direct verification on the presentation. Extend the normalized definition's candidate free-algebra substitution H_s ↦ H_s−(v⁻¹−v). The quadratic relation makes its quotient image H_s⁻¹ and gives the semilinearly conjugate quadratic relation. The braid relator is a palindrome, so its inverse is the braid relator for the inverse generators; distant inverse generators commute. The assignment therefore descends, is unique on generators, and squares to the identity. Reverse a reduced word to obtain the formula on H_w. No Choice is used.

items.title: Basic properties of the Bruhat order on $S_n$
items.statement: Let ≤ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based S_n of def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group, and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by 1. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers x→tx where t is a transposition and ℓ(tx)=ℓ(x)+1. (b) If y≤w then ℓ(y)≤ℓ(w), with equality iff y=w; every saturated chain has ℓ(w)−ℓ(y) steps; and y≤w iff y⁻¹≤w⁻¹. (c) y≤w iff for every reduced expression w=s_{i1}⋯s_{ik}, y is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection s, if y≤w and ℓ(sy)>ℓ(y), then y≤sw; if y≤w and ℓ(sw)<ℓ(w), then sy≤w. (e) Every interval [y,w] is finite; if y≤w, then [y,w]={y}∪⋃_{y→a≤w}[a,w].
items.strategy: Compare rank numbers and inversion-count transposition covers. Prove cross and paired-descent rank lifting by the threshold-i windows and adjacent thresholds i-1,i+1. Induct on the sum of lengths. In the paired-descent case, su<=sv gives an already constructed strong chain; the independently proved finite-Weyl subword equivalence gives a reduced subword su in a fixed reduced expression sv, and prefixing s gives a reduced subword u in v and hence a strong chain. That existing declared supplier has a complete local strong-exchange/subword proof, not an imported equivalence. Derive length, inversion symmetry, reduced subwords, both lifting cases and the finite interval-cover union, including its empty diagonal union. No Choice is used.

items.title: Bruhat intervals and the $R$-coefficients
items.statement: Let n≥1 and y,w∈S_n, identifying the zero-based rank-order model with the one-based Hecke model by shifting inputs and values by 1. The finite Bruhat interval [y,w]={z∈S_n:y≤z≤w} uses the order of [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]] and [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]]. Define the R-coefficients r_{y,w} by the unique standard-basis expansion ι(H_w)=H_{w⁻¹}⁻¹=Σ_{y∈S_n} r_{y,w}H_y in the normalization of [[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]; the sum is finite since S_n is finite. In rank one r_{id,s_i}=v−v⁻¹. The support, diagonal, and parity properties are stated and proved in [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]].
items.strategy: Definition item. The bar involution maps H_w into H_v(n), and the standard basis gives unique finite coefficients. The rank-one coefficient follows from H_s⁻¹=H_s−(v⁻¹−v). The later R-polynomial theorem proves support, diagonal, and parity properties. No Choice is used.

items.title: Reversal anti-involution commutes with the Hecke bar
items.statement: The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.
items.strategy: Extend reversal of words from the free algebra; check the quadratic, braid, and commutation relators; then verify the two compositions agree on coefficients and generators.

items.title: The $R$-coefficient recursion, support, degree bounds and inversion
items.statement: For $n\ge1$, let $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the $R$-coefficients of [[def-bruhat-interval-and-r-polynomials]]. (a) **Recursion.** Let $w\in S_n$ and let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection with $sw<w$. Then for every $y\in S_n$ $$r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}\quad\text{if }sy<y,\qquad r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}+(v-v^{-1})\,r_{y,sw}\quad\text{if }sy>y .$$ (b) **Support.** $r_{y,w}\ne0$ implies $y\le w$, and $r_{w,w}=1$. (c) **Degree and parity.** For $y\le w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $r_{y,w}\in v^{-d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{2},v^{-2}]$; the term of least $v$-degree is $\mathrm{sgn}(y)\,\mathrm{sgn}(w)\,v^{-d}$, and the term of largest $v$-degree is $v^{d}$. (d) **Symmetry.** $\overline{r_{y,w}}=\mathrm{sgn}(y)\mathrm{sgn}(w)r_{y,w}$ and $r_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=r_{y,w}$. (e) **Matrix inversion.** $\sum_{y\in S_n} r_{x,y}\,\overline{r_{y,z}}=\delta_{x,z}$ for all $x,z$; equivalently the triangular matrices $R=(r_{x,y})$, $\bar R$ satisfy $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$. Here $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$ and all coefficients are kept in the variable $v$ of this page.
items.strategy: (a) Derive the left generator multiplication rule from the presentation, expand $\iota(H_sH_{sw})$ and compare standard-basis coefficients; use the resulting recursion for (b)–(d). (b) Induct on $\ell(w)$ and use the reduced-subword characterization for each recursion branch. (c) Track parity and both extreme terms in the same induction. (d) Induct on the recursion for bar symmetry and apply [[lem-reversal-anti-involution-commutes-with-hecke-bar]] for inverse-index symmetry. (e) Apply $\iota^2=1$ to the coefficient expansion and then apply coefficient bar for the other matrix identity. All inductions are finite; no Choice is used.

items.title: The type-A Kazhdan–Lusztig basis has elementary triangular bar properties
items.statement: For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.
items.strategy: direct

references.locator: Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.4 and section 5.6; elementary triangular bar construction in the inverted-parameter convention

items.title: Verma's sign identity over Bruhat intervals
items.statement: For all $x<z$ in $S_n$, with $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$, $$\sum_{y\in S_n,\ x\le y\le z}\mathrm{sgn}(y)=0 .$$
items.strategy: By [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]](e), for $x<z$ the sum $\sum_y r_{x,y}\overline{r_{y,z}}$ is zero. Its bar symmetry (d) turns this into $\sum_y\mathrm{sgn}(y)r_{x,y}r_{y,z}=0$ after multiplying by $\mathrm{sgn}(z)$, and support (b) restricts to $y\in[x,z]$. Let $d=\ell(z)-\ell(x)$. The coefficient of $v^{-d}$ in each signed product is $\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(z)\mathrm{sgn}(y)$: the two lowest R-coefficients contribute $\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(z)$, and the outer factor contributes $\mathrm{sgn}(y)$. No other exponents contribute at degree $-d$. Thus the coefficient of $v^{-d}$ in the zero sum is $\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(z)\sum_{x\le y\le z}\mathrm{sgn}(y)$, proving the assertion. The Bruhat interval is finite by [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]], and no choice principle is used.

items.title: Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials in the classical $q$-normalization
items.statement:
Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].
items.strategy: A definition item. The well-definedness obligation is that $P_{y,w}\in\mathbb Z[q]$: this follows from the parity clause $p_{y,w}\in v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. Its leading coefficient and degree bound follow from the corresponding degree statement there. The $q$-normalization and dictionary are Elias–Williamson, Remark 3.2, and the two descriptions of $\mu$ agree because $q=v^{-2}$. No choice principle is used.

items.title: Multiplication by a generator in the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
items.statement: Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.
items.strategy: Prove the left ascent case by comparing standard-basis coefficients in $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ with $\underline H_{sw}+\sum_{sz<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$. The coefficient formula follows from the presented generator multiplication. When $sy<y$, the $z=y$ term cancels the constant term of $v^{-1}p_{y,w}$ because $\mu(y,w)$ is its coefficient of $v$; all other terms lie in $v\mathbb Z[v]$. When $sy>y$, induction on $\ell(w)$ gives $p_{y,z}=v p_{sy,z}$ for lower left descents and reduces the coefficient to $v f_{sy}+v p_{sy,sw}-p_{y,sw}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$; treat $y=w$ separately. The difference is bar-fixed and strictly lower, so uniqueness forces it to vanish. For $sw<w$, apply the ascent case to $sw$ and $(H_s-v^{-1})\underline H_s=0$, using induction on lower terms. Apply the reversal anti-automorphism to the left formulas for $w^{-1}$ to obtain the right formulas. The unresolved positivity clause of the basis supplier is not used; that supplier remains escalated. No choice principle is used.

items.title: The Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial descent recursion
items.statement: Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection, $w\in S_n$ with $sw<w$, and $y\le w$. With $P_{x,z}:=0$ whenever $x\not\le z$, $$P_{y,w}(q)=q^{1-c}P_{sy,sw}(q)+q^{c}P_{y,sw}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{y\le z\le sw\\ sz<z,\ \mu(z,sw)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(z,sw)\,q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2}P_{y,z}(q),$$ where $c=1$ if $sy<y$ and $c=0$ if $sy>y$; here $\mu$ is the coefficient defined in [[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]] (so the summand only occurs for $\ell(sw)-\ell(z)$ odd, and $(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2$ is then an integer). The same recursion holds with $s\in R(w)$ (right descents) after replacing each index $x$ by $x^{-1}$, using $P_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=P_{y,w}$ and $\mu(y^{-1},w^{-1})=\mu(y,w)$.
items.strategy: For the left descent sw<w, apply the KL-basis multiplication formula to the ascent product H̲_s H̲_{sw} and compare H_y coefficients after expanding in the standard basis. Derive the needed left standard-basis multiplication from reduced words and the quadratic relation. Convert the resulting p-coefficient equation using p_{x,z}=v^{ℓ(z)-ℓ(x)}P_{x,z}(v^{-2}); the μ parity clause makes each correction exponent integral. Obtain the right-descent formula by applying the left formula to inverse indices and using Bruhat inversion and inverse-index coefficient symmetry. All intervals and sums are finite; no Choice is used.

items.title: Inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials
items.statement:
For $x,w\in S_n$ set $$q'_{x,w}:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m\sum_{x=z_0<z_1<\cdots<z_m=w}p_{z_0,z_1}p_{z_1,z_2}\cdots p_{z_{m-1},z_m}\in A,$$ where the inner sum is over strictly increasing Bruhat chains from $x$ to $w$, the $m=0$ chain occurs only when $x=w$, and $p_{u,v}$ are the coefficients of the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]). Every chain lies in a finite Bruhat interval by [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]], so the sum is finite. If $x\not\le w$ there are no chains; if $x=w$, the empty chain gives $q'_{w,w}=1$. If $x<w$, each chain has at least one factor $p_{u,v}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ with $u<v$, so $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$.

Let $P=(p_{x,w})$ and $Q'=(q'_{x,w})$. The matrix $N:=P-I$ is strictly triangular on the finite Bruhat poset, hence nilpotent; the $(x,w)$ entry of $N^m$ is the sum of products over chains of $m$ strict steps. Therefore $$Q'=I-N+N^2-\cdots+(-1)^M N^M=(I+N)^{-1}=P^{-1},$$ where $M$ can be any integer at least the maximum strict-chain length. In particular, $Q'P=PQ'=I$ and $$\sum_zq'_{x,z}p_{z,w}=\delta_{x,w}=\sum_zp_{x,z}q'_{z,w}.$$

The **inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials** in the classical sign convention are $q_{x,w}:=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$. If $\Sigma$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $\Sigma_{x,x}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)$, then $Q=(q_{x,w})=\Sigma Q'\Sigma$. Equivalently, if $D_x$ is the basis of $H^*=\mathrm{Hom}_A(H,A)$ dual to the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis, then $$q'_{x,w}=D_x(H_w),$$ since $H_w=\sum_zq'_{z,w}\underline H_z$.
items.strategy: The chain sum is finite because each chain lies in the finite Bruhat interval [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]](e). Its diagonal term is the empty chain, equal to 1; for $x\not\le w$ no chain exists; and for $x<w$ every chain has at least one factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, so $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$. Let $N=P-I$. Since $P$ is unitriangular on the finite Bruhat poset, $N$ is nilpotent, and the chain sum is the entrywise finite sum $Q'=I-N+N^2-\cdots$, hence $Q'P=PQ'=I$. This also identifies $q'_{x,w}=D_x(H_w)$ for the functionals dual to the KL basis. The sign convention is $Q=sQ's$. No choice principle is used.

items.title: The Kazhdan–Lusztig inversion formula
items.statement: Let $P=(p_{x,w})$, $Q'=(q'_{x,w})$ and $R=(r_{x,y})$ be the triangular matrices of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]], [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] and [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]]. Then (a) $P=R\bar P$, $\bar P=\bar RP$, and $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$; (b) $Q'P=PQ'=1$, and the inversion formulas $$\overline{q'_{x,w}}=\sum_{x\le z\le w}q'_{x,z}r_{z,w},\qquad \overline{q_{x,w}}=\sum_{x\le z\le w}q_{x,z}\overline{r_{z,w}}$$ hold, i.e. $\bar Q'=Q'R$ and $\bar Q=Q\bar R$; (c) for the dual basis $D_x(\underline H_w)=\delta_{x,w}$ from [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]], $D_x(H_w)=q'_{x,w}$. The inversion is proved from the bar-duality relations alone (no finite case check).
items.strategy: (a) $P=R\bar P$ is bar-duality from [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]; applying bar gives $\bar P=\bar RP$, and $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$ is from [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]]. (b) By [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]], $Q'=P^{-1}$. Inverting $P=R\bar P$ gives $Q'=\bar Q'\bar R$, hence $\bar Q'=Q'R$. With the sign matrix $S^2=1$, $Q=SQ'S$ and $\bar R=SRS$ give $\bar Q=Q\bar R$. (c) The coordinate functionals dual to the KL basis have standard-basis values given by $Q'$. All matrices are finite because $S_n$ is finite; no choice principle is used.

items.title: $L$-, $R$- and two-sided Kazhdan–Lusztig preorders and cells
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $C_w:=\underline H_w$ be the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis from [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]], and let $S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_{n-1}\}$ be the simple reflections of $S_n$. For $x,y\in S_n$, write $x\leftarrow_L y$ if the coefficient of $C_x$ in $C_sC_y$ is nonzero for some $s\in S$, and write $x\leftarrow_R y$ if the coefficient of $C_x$ in $C_yC_s$ is nonzero for some $s\in S$. Define $x\le_L y$ if there is a finite chain $x=w_0,\ldots,w_m=y$ with $w_i\leftarrow_Lw_{i+1}$ for every $i<m$; define $\le_R$ using $\leftarrow_R$, and define $\le_{LR}$ by allowing either kind of step at each place. The length-zero chain makes each relation reflexive. Define $x\sim_Ly$ by $x\le_Ly$ and $y\le_Lx$, and similarly $\sim_R$ and $\sim_{LR}$. Their equivalence classes are the **left cells**, **right cells**, and **two-sided cells**.

For $w\in S_n$, set $L(w):=\{s\in S:sw<w\}$ and $R(w):=\{s\in S:ws<w\}$. The recorded properties are: $\le_L,\le_R,\le_{LR}$ are preorders; $x\le_Ly$ iff $x^{-1}\le_Ry^{-1}$; $x\le_Ly$ implies $R(y)\subseteq R(x)$ and $x\le_Ry$ implies $L(y)\subseteq L(x)$; consequently, elements of one left cell have equal right descent sets and elements of one right cell have equal left descent sets.

The multiplication formula [[thm-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-multiplication-formula]] gives the non-diagonal elementary left steps: if $sw>w$, then $C_{sw}$ occurs with coefficient $1$, and $C_z$ occurs with coefficient $\mu(z,w)$ exactly for the terms $z<w$, $sz<z$, and $\mu(z,w)\ne0$. If $sw<w$, the product is $(v+v^{-1})C_w$, so it gives only a diagonal step. (That diagonal coefficient is nonzero, but it adds no relation beyond the length-zero chain.)
items.strategy: Reflexivity comes from length-zero chains and transitivity from concatenation. The reversal anti-automorphism sends each Kazhdan–Lusztig basis vector to the vector indexed by its inverse, so it carries every elementary left coefficient to the corresponding right coefficient and yields inversion symmetry. For a left coefficient a_x of C_x in C_s C_y, t in R(y) gives (C_s C_y) C_t=(v+v^{-1})C_s C_y. If xt>x, the right multiplication formula makes the coefficient of C_x on the left zero: a leading term could reach x only from the descent index xt, and all lower corrections have t-descent indices. Thus a_x=0 since v+v^{-1} is nonzero in Z[v^{±1}]. The left-eigenvector argument gives the right-preorder descent inclusion. Mutual reachability gives equality of descent sets within cells. Finally, split the multiplication formula into its ascent and descent cases; in the descent case retain the nonzero diagonal coefficient while noting there are no non-diagonal steps. The proof is finite and uses no choice principle.

items.title: Knuth and dual Knuth equivalence for permutations
items.statement: Fix n≥1 and write S_n in the 1-based convention of def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n. Its zero-based realization in def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation is identified by the order-preserving shift on inputs and values. For a<b<c, allow the reversible contiguous-factor moves bca↔bac and cab↔acb. Knuth equivalence is the equivalence relation generated by finite chains of these moves (including length zero); dual Knuth equivalence is Knuth equivalence after inversion. The insertion tableau P(x) is obtained by row-inserting the one-line word of x from the empty tableau. Every elementary move preserves P, and two permutations are Knuth equivalent iff their insertion tableaux agree; this well-definedness/result is supplied by thm-knuth-equivalence-classes-are-insertion-tableau-fibers.
items.strategy: Definition item. The two reversible moves generate an equivalence relation: zero-length chains give reflexivity, reversing a chain gives symmetry, and concatenating chains gives transitivity. Inversion is a bijection, so it transports this equivalence relation to the dual one. The order-preserving shift between the two S_n conventions preserves all comparisons. The row-insertion definition supplies P; the assigned Knuth-fiber theorem establishes its invariance and the exact fiber characterization. No Choice is used.

items.title: Knuth classes are the fibers of the insertion tableau
items.statement: For permutations x,y∈S_n with RSK pairs (P(x),Q(x)) and (P(y),Q(y)), x∼_K y iff P(x)=P(y), and x∼_{dK}y iff Q(x)=Q(y). Thus the Knuth and dual Knuth classes are exactly the insertion- and recording-tableau fibers, and the induced maps from classes to standard tableaux of size n are bijections.
items.strategy: Direct row-bumping proof. Check the two Knuth relations on one increasing row: in each pair the final row agrees and the bumped words are either equal or another Knuth pair; induction down rows uses the proved standardness of each output. For the converse, read a tableau bottom-to-top, left-to-right: one insertion transforms the old row word to the new one by explicit Knuth moves along the bumping position. Induct on word length to connect every word to its tableau row word. RSK inversion symmetry gives the recording-tableau fiber statement, and the RSK bijection gives surjectivity of both class maps. No Choice is used.

items.title: Star operations on strings of adjacent simple reflections
items.statement: For n≥3 and r=s_i,t=s_{i+1}, let D_i={w∈S_n: exactly one of r,t is a right descent}. In each right coset of ⟨r,t⟩≅S_3, sort the entries in positions i,i+1,i+2 increasingly to obtain its unique shortest element w̃. The six elements are w̃, w̃r, w̃t, w̃rt, w̃tr, w̃rtr with lengths ℓ(w̃)+0,…,ℓ(w̃)+3; D_i consists of w̃r,w̃rt,w̃t,w̃tr. Define the right star involution by w̃r↔w̃rt and w̃t↔w̃tr. Define the left star on D_i⁻¹ by *w=((w⁻¹)^*)⁻¹. In one-line notation the two pairs are bac↔bca and acb↔cab, so w and w* differ by one Knuth move on positions i,i+1,i+2.
items.strategy: Definition item. The right coset permutes a consecutive three-position block. Its unique shortest representative sorts the three distinct entries: all inversions with positions outside the block have unchanged total contribution, while the internal inversion count is uniquely minimized at the sorted triple. The six S3 patterns have lengths 0,1,1,2,2,3 relative to this representative; exactly the four length-1 and length-2 patterns have one right descent. Pairing them as r↔rt and t↔tr defines an involution. The four one-line patterns are bac, bca, acb, cab and the paired moves are exactly the two Knuth relations. The left operation is conjugated by inversion.

items.title: Star operations are Knuth moves and preserve the relevant cells
items.statement: Let $D_i$ and $(-)^*$ be as in [[def-star-operations-on-the-symmetric-group]]. (a) For $w\in D_i$, $w^*$ is obtained from $w$ by one elementary Knuth relation on the letters in positions $i,i+1,i+2$; in particular $P(w^*)=P(w)$. Put $D_{ij}:=\{w\in D_i:ws_i<w,\ ws_{i+1}>w\}$ and $D_{ji}:=\{w\in D_i:ws_i>w,\ ws_{i+1}<w\}$. The restriction $K_{ij}$ of $(-)^*$ is a bijection $D_{ij}\to D_{ji}$ whose inverse is $K_{ji}$. (b) For every $w\in D_i$, if $a$ and $b$ are the shorter and longer, respectively, of $\{w,w^*\}$, then $\mu(a,b)=1$ and $w^*\sim_Rw$; by inversion, $^*w\sim_Lw$ whenever $w^{-1}\in D_i$. (c) Inside the rank-two subgroup $W_I=\langle s_i,s_{i+1}\rangle\cong S_3$, every Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial $P_{x,y}$ with $x\le y$ is $1$, and $\mu(x,y)=1$ exactly for Bruhat covers $x\lessdot y$. For every shortest representative $\widetilde w$ of a right $W_I$-coset, the ambient pairs $\widetilde w s_i\lessdot\widetilde w s_i s_{i+1}$ and $\widetilde w s_{i+1}\lessdot\widetilde w s_{i+1}s_i$ therefore also have $\mu$-coefficient $1$.
items.strategy: Part (a) follows from the one-line star table and the Knuth-fiber theorem. For the rank-two calculation, compute the six A2 basis elements inside the subgroup from the multiplication formula and standard quadratic relation; this gives P=1 and cover mu-coefficients. In the ambient group, each pair related by the star table is a Bruhat cover, so the basis theorem gives p=v and hence mu=1. For each pair, the ascent multiplication formula gives one right coefficient edge with coefficient 1; the opposite edge is the mu-term in multiplication by the other generator, since the upper star element ascends and the lower one descends. Thus the pair is right-cell equivalent. Inversion gives the left-star statement. The full global KL basis of an arbitrary shifted coset is not asserted to be supported in that coset.

items.title: $\mu$-edges and left equivalence are transported by star operations
items.statement:
Fix $i$, let $D_{ij},D_{ji},K_{ij}$ be as in [[lem-dual-knuth-star-operations-give-antiparallel-kazhdan-lusztig-graph-edges]], and write $\mu(u|v)$ for $\mu(u,v)$ if $u<v$, for $\mu(v,u)$ if $v<u$, and for $0$ otherwise, so its nonzero predicate agrees with [[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]. (a) **Edge transport.** For $y,w\in D_{ij}$ with $y
e w$ and $\mu(y|w)
e0$ one has $\mu(K_{ij}(y)|K_{ij}(w))
e0$, and in fact the transported leading coefficients agree: $\mu(K_{ij}(y)|K_{ij}(w))=\mu(y|w)$, the transported pair being taken in the Bruhat order in which it is comparable. (b) **Transport of the preorder.** For $x,y\in D_{ij}$: $x\le_Ly\iff K_{ij}(x)\le_LK_{ij}(y)$ and $x\le_Ry\iff K_{ij}(x)\le_RK_{ij}(y)$; in particular $x\sim_Ly\iff K_{ij}(x)\sim_LK_{ij}(y)$ and $x\sim_Ry\iff K_{ij}(x)\sim_RK_{ij}(y)$.
items.strategy: (a) Put $\pi_{a,b}=p_{a,b}/v$. Derive the right-descent recursion from [[thm-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomial-recursion]] and mixed-descent vanishing from [[thm-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-multiplication-formula]]. Handle the same-coset covers directly; for distinct cosets compare constant terms in the two recursion cases, with the complete symmetric orientation recorded in Casselman, Theorem 6.2, §§4.4–4.5 and §5.3. (b) Right-preorder transport follows from the elementwise right-cell equivalence in [[lem-dual-knuth-star-operations-give-antiparallel-kazhdan-lusztig-graph-edges]](b). For left-preorder transport, let $I_s,I_t$ be the spans of KL basis elements with the respective right descents and $J=I_s\cap I_t$. Right multiplication by the adjacent KL generator induces inverse left-module maps $I_s/J\leftrightarrow I_t/J$ and sends each quotient basis element to its star. The mixed-descent coefficient identity proves the basis action locally. Right-descent monotonicity traps every intermediate element of a left-preorder chain in the one-sided domain. No p-canonical basis or Choice is used.

items.title: Equal insertion or recording tableaux imply right or left equivalence
items.statement: For $x,y\in S_n$: (a) $P(x)=P(y)\Rightarrow x\sim_Ry$; (b) $Q(x)=Q(y)\Rightarrow x\sim_Ly$. Equivalently: a Knuth class lies in a single right cell and a dual Knuth class lies in a single left cell.
items.strategy: (b) By the symmetry theorem $P(w^{-1})=Q(w)$ ([[cor-rsk-symmetry-under-inversion]]), $Q(x)=Q(y)$ gives $P(x^{-1})=P(y^{-1})$, so $x^{-1},y^{-1}$ are Knuth equivalent ([[thm-knuth-equivalence-classes-are-insertion-tableau-fibers]]); a chain of elementary Knuth moves joins them, each move is a right star step on the corresponding domain ([[def-star-operations-on-the-symmetric-group]]), and each such step stays in a right cell ([[lem-dual-knuth-star-operations-give-antiparallel-kazhdan-lusztig-graph-edges]](b)); hence $x^{-1}\sim_Ry^{-1}$, and inversion gives $x\sim_Ly$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-kazhdan-lusztig-preorders-and-cells]]). (a) is the same argument applied to $x^{-1},y^{-1}$ and the dual-Knuth half of [[thm-knuth-equivalence-classes-are-insertion-tableau-fibers]], or directly by inversion. This is [Ariki, Proposition 3.8]. No choice principle is used.

items.title: Left equivalence forces equality of recording tableaux in type A
items.statement: For $x,y\in S_n$: $x\sim_Ly\Rightarrow Q(x)=Q(y)$.
items.strategy: Prove locally that adjacent descents of the word are exactly the descent positions of its recording tableau, and that among standard tableaux of the fixed shape lambda, the column-superstandard tableau is determined by its descent set, using containment in that final shape to exclude additions below already complete columns. Replace each endpoint by the unique permutation with its column-superstandard insertion tableau and the same recording tableau, using [[prop-same-insertion-or-recording-tableaux-imply-cell-equivalence]]. Join each replacement to the diagonal RSK permutation by a Knuth path; carry both paths across the other endpoint using the rank-two star operation and [[lem-kazhdan-lusztig-mu-edges-and-left-cells-are-transported-by-star-operations]](b). Compare the resulting column-block lengths from their equal right descent sets, then explicitly obtain shape(Q(w_prime))=lambda from the locally compared insertion shapes and RSK common shape, and use the fixed-shape descent correspondence and RSK uniqueness to identify the recording tableaux. Ariki, §3.4, is the source route; no choice principle is used.

items.title: Kazhdan–Lusztig cells of type A are classified by RSK tableaux
items.statement: For $x,y\in S_n$, with the RSK tableaux $P,Q$ of [[thm-robinson-schensted-correspondence]] (insertion tableau and recording tableau of the one-line word): $$x\sim_Ly\iff Q(x)=Q(y),\qquad x\sim_Ry\iff P(x)=P(y),\qquad x\sim_{LR}y\iff \operatorname{sh}(Q(x))=\operatorname{sh}(Q(y)).$$ Here $\sim_L,\sim_R,\sim_{LR}$ are the cell equivalence relations of [[def-left-right-and-two-sided-kazhdan-lusztig-preorders-and-cells]]; the chosen convention is displayed: **left cells are the fibers of the recording tableau**, **right cells are the fibers of the insertion tableau**, and **two-sided cells are the fibers of the shape map** (note $\operatorname{sh}(P(w))=\operatorname{sh}(Q(w))$). Consequently the left cells of $S_n$ are in bijection with the standard tableaux of size $n$, the right cells likewise, and the two-sided cells with the partitions of $n$.
items.strategy: Left classification uses the local recording-tableau implication and converse. Right classification follows by inversion and RSK symmetry. For two-sided equivalence implies equal shape, invoke only Geck Corollary5.6(c)'s authorized forward implication, after locally checking u=v^-1, relations/bar, triangular-basis uniqueness and nonzero simple-product coefficient/preorder-chain correspondence. Equal shape implies two-sided equivalence by the unique RSK preimage of (P(x),Q(y)). Counts use local RSK surjectivity and canonical standard tableaux. No stronger tableau-dominance premise or local Murphy/leading-matrix proof is claimed. No Choice is used.

items.title: The real type-A Soergel category by scalar extension
items.statement:
**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric form that is $S$-bilinear for the right action and invariant under
the left action in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.
items.strategy: The place permutation action and coordinate roots/coroots are explicitly supplied by the published two-normalization realization. We fix the coordinate choice for every alpha, Demazure trace and positivity condition on this Hodge page. The invariant-ring tensor bimodules do not change when a root is multiplied by -1; only the chosen Demazure/trace normalization changes, so no diagrammatic presentation is silently reinterpreted. The polynomial ring has S_0=R and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces. Flat extension of Q to R commutes with the finite free presentations, invariant decomposition S=S^{s_i}⊕alpha_i S^{s_i}, shifts and tensor products. The idempotent closure is the defined real category; preservation of rational indecomposable labels is proved separately in the comparison lemma. For rho=Σ c_jx_j, rho(alpha_i^vee)=c_i-c_{i+1}; the displayed decreasing coefficients give value 1 at every simple coroot. These are the positive roots x_a-x_b for a<b used by inversion length, with adjacent Cartan entries -1. No alternating-sign dominant chamber or unverified replacement of rho is used.

items.title: The Hecke trace form, its values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis, and the standard pairing
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** induction on the length in the standard basis; the ambient algebra is finite free over $A$.

1.1 **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2). [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$. [base, step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 **The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below. [step 2.1, F1, F2]

4.1 **The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$. [step 3.1, ih]

5.1 **The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$. [step 4.1, ih]

6.1 **The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 **Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4). [step 6.1, F2]

7.2 **The generator trace identity.** By step 6.1, for every $w$ and simple reflection $s$ one has $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\delta_{w,s^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_sH_w)=\delta_{s,w^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$. Extending over the standard basis gives $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$. In particular the common value for $w=s$ is $1$. [step 6.1, F1, algebra]

8.1 **$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$. [step 7.2, F2, algebra]

8.2 **Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. A nonzero term requires $u\le x$ and $u\le y$; if $x\ne y$, every surviving term has a factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, because $u<x$ or $u<y$ is [F3], and $u=x\ne y$ gives $h_{x,y}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ when $x<y$ and $h_{x,y}=0$ otherwise, symmetrically for $u=y$; hence $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $x\ne y$. For $x=y$ the term $u=x$ contributes $h_{x,x}^2=1$ and every other term has $u<x$ and contributes to $v^2\mathbb Z[v]$, so $(\underline H_x,\underline H_x)\in 1+v\mathbb Z[v]$. [step 7.1, F3, algebra]

9.1 **The standard pairing (6) and conclusion.** By (4) the form $(-,-)$ is the $A$-bilinear form whose matrix in the normalized standard basis $\{H_x\}$ is the identity; the published type-A Soergel Hom formula uses the standard pairing with $\langle H_x,H_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$ on that normalized basis, and the dictionary of [F4] fixes the normalization $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and the resulting Kazhdan-Lusztig coefficients, so the transported pairing agrees with $(-,-)$ on the basis and hence on $H$ by bilinearity. All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice. [step 8.1, step 8.2, F3, F4, discharge-induction: step 5.1] ∎

items.title: Indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodules are classified by their normalized top support
items.statement: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.
items.strategy:
1.1 A finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra and the absence of nontrivial idempotents imply locality. Indeed for an endomorphism $f$ its polynomial minimal relation splits into a power of $T$ and a factor coprime to $T$. The polynomial Chinese remainder identity produces an idempotent separating the nilpotent and invertible parts; indecomposability forces one part to vanish. Thus every $f$ is invertible or nilpotent, and a nonunit $f$ has $1-f$ invertible. Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer. [F2, step 3.1, choose]

5.1 Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1]

6.1 If $M$ is indecomposable, step 5.1 gives $M\cong B_x(d)$. If two normalized candidates were obtained from different reduced expressions for $x$, applying that same splitting argument to either candidate makes them isomorphic, because their normalized rank-one top degrees force $d=0$. Distinct labels cannot be isomorphic, by their maximal support; distinct shifts at a fixed label cannot be isomorphic, by their top generator degrees. This proves classification and reduced-word independence. [step 3.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Restriction of degree-zero endomorphisms of $B_x$ to its rank-one top layer is a unital homomorphism onto $k$, since homogeneous scalars act there and its endomorphism ring in degree zero is $k$. Its kernel is a maximal ideal. Locality in step 1.1 makes this the unique maximal ideal, so the residue field is $k$. All selections were from finite supports and finite homogeneous bases, and no choice axiom beyond finite choice is used. The statement follows from steps 2.1, 3.1, 6.1 and this residue calculation. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1] ∎

items.title: Normalized type-A Soergel bimodules are self-dual and have length degree bounds
items.statement: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.
items.strategy:
1.1 The unit has the perfect multiplication form. If a right-free bimodule $M$ has an invariant form, put $a(b)=b c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $b(b')=b'c_s$ in $MB_s$ and define the induced form by $\langle a(u),a(v)\rangle=\partial_s\langle u,v\rangle$, $\langle a(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle b(u),a(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$, and $\langle b(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\alpha_s$. Extend on a right basis by right bilinearity. The relation of [F2] and the identity $\partial_s(fr)=\partial_s(f)r+s(f)\partial_s(r)$ verify that these formulas agree for arbitrary $u,v$, and that left multiplication is self-adjoint. Symmetry follows from symmetry of the preceding form. If $e_i,e_i^*$ are dual right bases for that form, the pairing between bases $(a(e_i),b(e_i))$ and $(b(e_i^*),a(e_i^*))$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\\alpha_sI&I\end{pmatrix}$, using $\partial_s(1)=0$, and has determinant one. Thus perfection is preserved. Iteration yields a perfect symmetric invariant form on every word, exactly its successive rank-one trace multiplication form. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For finite right-free modules the graded double-dual evaluation is an isomorphism, so $D$ is an involutive contravariant equivalence and takes indecomposables to indecomposables. The invariant perfect word form of step 1.1 identifies a word with its right dual. Generic graph support is unchanged by this duality: in a right basis left multiplication matrices transpose under $D$, so their simultaneous eigencharacters, and hence the graph labels after passing to the polynomial fraction field, are unchanged. A right-free summand has precisely the support closure of those graph labels. Therefore $DB_x$ is an indecomposable summand with the $x$ graph of the same reduced word. Uniqueness in [F1] identifies it with $B_x$ with no shift. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A word of length $m$ has a homogeneous right basis given by tensor products of the two basis elements in [F2]; its generator degrees lie between $-m$ and $m$ and have parity $m$. Right reduction preserves a split direct-sum decomposition. Since $B_x$ is an unshifted summand of its reduced word of length $m=\ell(x)$, its reduction has these same bounds and parity. The word's bottom degree is the single $1$-tensor. The balanced evaluation of that word on its top graph, obtained by successively twisting the tensor-slot polynomials by the successive prefix permutations, sends this $1$-tensor to $1$. It factors through the rank-one top quotient, and is an isomorphism onto $R_x(m)$ because both generators have degree $-m$. All other summands have no $x$ support; consequently the projection of the bottom tensor into $B_x$ is nonzero. Its bottom dimension is therefore one. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Right duality reverses the degrees of the finite homogeneous basis after reduction. The unshifted duality $DB_x\cong B_x$ from step 2.1 therefore makes the reduced dimensions symmetric and gives top dimension one from the bottom dimension in step 3.1. The perfect trace forms, duality, degree bounds, parity and extremal dimensions have now all been established locally. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎
